name: Diamond-Blackfan anaemia
aliases: pure red cell aplasia of infancy

reference.source: OMIM / GeneReviews (NCBI) and inherited bone-marrow-failure consensus guidance
clinicalPearls: Inherited ribosomopathy causing a congenital pure red cell aplasia, frequently caused by variants in ribosomal protein genes such as RPS19
Typically presents in the first year of life with severe macrocytic anaemia, reticulocytopenia and a normal white cell and platelet count
Bone marrow shows a selective paucity of erythroid precursors with otherwise normal cellularity
Around half of patients have congenital anomalies, including craniofacial (Cathie facies), thumb (triphalangeal or duplicated), cardiac and genitourinary defects, and short stature
Raised erythrocyte adenosine deaminase activity and elevated fetal haemoglobin support the diagnosis
Corticosteroids induce a response in many patients; others become dependent on long-term red cell transfusion with attendant iron overload
There is an increased risk of myelodysplastic syndrome, acute leukaemia and solid tumours over a lifetime
Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation can cure the haematological disease and is used for transfusion dependence or clonal progression
reference.pathophysiology: Diamond-Blackfan anaemia is caused by haploinsufficiency of genes encoding ribosomal proteins, impairing ribosome biogenesis. Disrupted assembly of the ribosomal subunits activates stabilisation of p53 and stress pathways to which erythroid progenitors are especially sensitive, producing selective failure of red cell production. The same ribosomal stress and secondary genomic instability contribute to the congenital malformations and the heightened risk of malignancy.
additionalDifferentials: Fanconi anaemia and other inherited marrow-failure syndromes
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and reticulocyte count showing macrocytic anaemia with reticulocytopenia
Bone marrow examination demonstrating erythroid hypoplasia
Molecular genetic testing of ribosomal protein genes
Assessment for congenital anomalies with echocardiography, renal imaging and limb radiographs
redFlags: Evolving neutropenia or thrombocytopenia suggesting progression to marrow failure or myelodysplasia
Clonal cytogenetic change or blasts indicating malignant transformation
Symptomatic iron overload from chronic transfusion
Severe anaemia with cardiovascular compromise at presentation
reference.prognosis: Many patients achieve stable disease with corticosteroids or transfusion support, and some undergo spontaneous remission; long-term outcome is influenced by transfusional iron overload and the lifelong increased risk of myelodysplasia, leukaemia and solid tumours. Transplantation is curative for the haematological disease.
pitfalls: Confusing it with transient erythroblastopenia of childhood, which recovers spontaneously
Overlooking parvovirus B19 as a cause of acute red cell aplasia
Failing to monitor and treat transfusional iron overload
